title: Acute Pancreatitis: Clues to Cause and Ranson Severity
summary: Use ALT, the lipase-to-amylase ratio and urine amylase for what they can and cannot tell you about the cause of acute pancreatitis, and score severity with the 11 Ranson criteria.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 23 Hit 4 (urine amylase), Hit 6 (ALT and lipase/amylase ratio for cause) and Hit 7 (Ranson criteria). Checked against Shah 2018, Hazem 2009, Ekka 2023, McCarrick 2025, Abu-Eshy 2008, Lee 2022, Hu 2023 and Skude 2000. Qualified: Hit 6’s “AST/ALT > 3× ULN means gallstones in 95%” is taught as ALT > 150 IU/L with ~95% PPV but ~48% sensitivity (rv-ap-alt-gallstone-sensitivity); the “ratio > 5, low sensitivity” is taught as the meta-analysed ~3 cut-off with modest specificity (rv-ap-lipase-amylase-ratio-cutoff); Hit 7 is the non-gallstone Ranson set, with a separate biliary set (rv-ranson-biliary-version); Hit 4’s “useful in late presenters” is not supported by a 2025 meta-analysis (rv-urine-amylase-late-presenters). Not taught: the > 1000 Somogyi units/hour urine amylase figure and the AST-alone version of Hit 6.

objectives: Interpret an ALT above 150 IU/L in acute pancreatitis and state why a normal ALT does not exclude gallstones.
State the limited accuracy of the lipase-to-amylase ratio and of urine amylase.
List the five admission and six 48-hour Ranson criteria and the severe threshold.

scenes.title: Two pancreatitis patients, two questions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two patients already diagnosed with acute pancreatitis. (1) A 62-year-old woman: ALT 410 IU/L, lipase raised. (2) A 45-year-old man who drinks heavily: lipase-to-amylase ratio 4, ALT normal; he arrived on day 5 of pain, and someone suggests a urine amylase. Question token: “What caused it, and how sick will they get?”

cues.text: Two patients already have a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. The first, a sixty-two-year-old woman, has an A L T of four hundred and ten.
The second, a heavy drinker, has a lipase-to-amylase ratio of four, a normal A L T, and arrived on day five. Someone asks for a urine amylase.
What caused each attack, and how will you predict who gets severely ill?

props.label: What caused it, and how sick will they get?

scenes.title: Where the clues come from
scenes.altText: Schematic: pancreas, liver and bile duct, salivary glands and kidney. Card “Causes”: gallstones are the most common cause (about half of UK cases in one review), alcohol the second. Card “Liver tests”: AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are reviewed to separate biliary from other causes. Card “Amylase sources”: total serum amylase comes from salivary glands and pancreas (about 40% pancreatic in one review; roughly equal in another). Card “Kidney”: amylase is cleared into urine; urine amylase follows the serum rise.

cues.text: Start with causes. Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis, about half of U K cases in one review, and alcohol is the second.
To separate a biliary cause from the others, the liver tests are reviewed: A S T, A L T, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin.
Amylase in serum is not only pancreatic. Salivary glands supply a large share: one review puts the pancreatic part near forty percent, another says the two sources are roughly equal.
The kidneys clear amylase into the urine, so urine amylase rises after serum amylase and stays up longer.

scenes.title: Clues to the cause
scenes.altText: ALT card: ALT > 150 IU/L (about threefold) during an attack has a positive predictive value of about 95% for gallstone pancreatitis in a meta-analysis; in another study its specificity was 96% but sensitivity only 48%, so a normal ALT does not exclude gallstones. Lipase/amylase card: the ratio was proposed in 1991 to separate alcoholic from non-alcoholic attacks; a 2023 meta-analysis (cut-off about 3) found pooled sensitivity 74% and specificity 63%, moderate accuracy — suggestive, not diagnostic. Urine amylase card: stays elevated longer than serum amylase, but a 2025 meta-analysis found it did not outperform serum amylase (sensitivity 80%, specificity 86% at a model-derived 1,373 IU/L) and its value in late presenters is unproven.

cues.text: A L T above one hundred and fifty units per litre, about three times normal, points to gallstones: one meta-analysis gives a positive predictive value of about ninety-five percent.
But it is insensitive. In one study, sensitivity was only forty-eight percent, so a normal A L T does not exclude gallstones.

The lipase-to-amylase ratio was proposed to flag alcohol. A 2023 meta-analysis, using a cut-off near three, found sensitivity seventy-four percent and specificity sixty-three percent: a hint, not a diagnosis.
Urine amylase stays up longer than serum amylase, but a 2025 meta-analysis found it no better than serum amylase, and its value in late presenters is unproven.

props.title: Urine amylase
lines: Not better than serum; late-presenter value unproven

scenes.title: Ranson: five at the door, six by 48 hours
scenes.altText: Ranson criteria (non-gallstone version). At admission: age > 55 y; WBC > 16,000/mm³; glucose > 200 mg/dL; LDH > 350 U/L; AST > 250 U/L. Within 48 h: haematocrit fall > 10 percentage points; BUN rise > 5 mg/dL; calcium < 8 mg/dL; PaO₂ < 60 mmHg; base deficit > 4 mEq/L; fluid sequestration > 6 L. One point each; ≥ 3 = severe. A biliary version uses different cut-offs (for example age > 70, WBC > 18,000, LDH > 400). Hook answers token: patient 1 — ALT points to gallstones; patient 2 — ratio only hints at alcohol, urine amylase adds little; both — score Ranson over 48 h.

cues.text: Ranson’s criteria score severity. Five are taken at admission: age over fifty-five, white cells over sixteen thousand, glucose over two hundred, L D H over three hundred and fifty, and A S T over two hundred and fifty.

Six more come within forty-eight hours: haematocrit falling more than ten points, B U N rising more than five, calcium under eight, P O two under sixty, base deficit over four, and fluid sequestration over six litres.
Each criterion scores one point, and three or more means severe. A separate gallstone version uses different cut-offs, such as age over seventy.
Back to the hook. The woman’s A L T points to gallstones. The man’s ratio only hints at alcohol, and urine amylase adds little. For both, score Ranson over forty-eight hours.

props.label: 1 point each · ≥ 3 = severe · biliary cut-offs differ
1: ALT → gallstones · 2: ratio only a hint · both: Ranson over 48 h

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal ALT rules out gallstone pancreatitis” (✓ ALT > 150 IU/L is specific but insensitive; a normal ALT does not exclude gallstones); “A high lipase/amylase ratio proves alcohol” (✓ pooled specificity only 63%; it is a hint); “Ranson can be completed at admission” (✓ six of the eleven criteria are measured within 48 hours).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal A L T rules out gallstones. No: A L T over one hundred and fifty is specific but insensitive.
Trap two: a high lipase-to-amylase ratio proves alcohol. No: its pooled specificity was only about sixty-three percent. It is a hint.
Trap three: Ranson is finished at admission. No: six of the eleven criteria need the first forty-eight hours.

scenes.title: GA-LAW at the door, C-HOBBS by 48 hours
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “At the door, the GA-LAW: Glucose, Age, LDH, AST, WBC. By 48 hours, C-HOBBS: Calcium, Hct, Oxygen, BUN, Base deficit, Sequestration.” Tokens: GA-LAW = admission five · C-HOBBS = 48-hour six. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: at the door, the GA-LAW: glucose, age, L D H, A S T and white cells. By forty-eight hours, C-HOBBS: calcium, haematocrit, oxygen, B U N, base deficit and sequestration.
Where it breaks: the letters carry no cut-offs, the gallstone version uses different numbers, and Ranson cannot be completed until forty-eight hours, so other scores are also used.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “ALT > 150 IU/L → gallstones likely, but normal ALT ≠ excluded · lipase/amylase ratio = hint only · urine amylase adds little”, “Ranson: 5 at admission + 6 within 48 h · ≥ 3 = severe”.

cues.text: An ALT above 150 units per litre strongly suggests gallstones but a normal one does not exclude them, the lipase-to-amylase ratio only hints at alcohol, urine amylase adds little, and Ranson needs five admission and six 48-hour criteria, with three or more meaning severe.

props.label: ALT > 150 → gallstones likely · ratio = hint · urine amylase adds little
Ranson: 5 at admission + 6 by 48 h · ≥ 3 = severe

explanation.what: Plain language: once pancreatitis is diagnosed, you ask why it happened and how bad it will get. A high liver enzyme (ALT) suggests a gallstone; a high lipase-to-amylase ratio only hints at alcohol; urine amylase adds little; and a point score taken at admission and over the next two days predicts severity. Scientific terms: alanine aminotransferase (ALT), positive predictive value, sensitivity, specificity, lipase/amylase (L/A) ratio, urinary amylase, Ranson criteria, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), base deficit, fluid sequestration.
explanation.why: Gallstones are the most common cause and alcohol the second; the cause changes management. Marker cut-offs that are specific but insensitive can confirm but not exclude. Ranson combines admission and 48-hour data, so the full score is only available after two days.
explanation.measure: ALT > 150 IU/L (about 3×): PPV ~95% for gallstones (meta-analysis); specificity 96%, sensitivity 48% (one study). L/A ratio ≥ ~3: pooled sensitivity 74%, specificity 63%. Urine amylase: sensitivity 80%, specificity 86% at a model-derived 1,373 IU/L; not better than serum amylase. Ranson admission: age > 55, WBC > 16,000/mm³, glucose > 200 mg/dL, LDH > 350 U/L, AST > 250 U/L; 48 h: Hct fall > 10 points, BUN rise > 5 mg/dL, Ca < 8 mg/dL, PaO₂ < 60 mmHg, base deficit > 4 mEq/L, fluid > 6 L; ≥ 3 = severe.
explanation.differs: Specific-but-insensitive ALT (rules in) vs the lipase/amylase ratio (weak either way); urine vs serum amylase; non-gallstone vs gallstone Ranson cut-offs; admission vs 48-hour criteria.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the likely cause after a high ALT, recognising a 48-hour vs admission Ranson criterion, the Ranson severe threshold, or a trap that treats a normal ALT or a ratio as definitive.

comparisons.title: ALT vs lipase/amylase ratio
comparisons.distinguisher: A high ALT rules gallstones in; the ratio neither rules in nor out.

mnemonic.text: At the door, the GA-LAW: Glucose, Age, LDH, AST, WBC. By 48 hours, C-HOBBS: Calcium, Hct, Oxygen, BUN, Base deficit, Sequestration.
mnemonic.explanation: Splits the 11 Ranson criteria into the five admission and six 48-hour items.
mnemonic.limitation: The letters carry no cut-offs; the gallstone version uses different numbers; Ranson cannot be completed until 48 hours, so other scores are also used.

analogyLimitations: Accuracy figures come from individual studies and meta-analyses; cut-offs and assays differ.
takeaway: An ALT above 150 units per litre strongly suggests gallstones but a normal one does not exclude them, the lipase-to-amylase ratio only hints at alcohol, urine amylase adds little, and Ranson needs five admission and six 48-hour criteria, with three or more meaning severe.

questions.stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis has an ALT of 410 IU/L on admission. Which cause is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. ALT above 150 IU/L (about threefold) has a positive predictive value of about 95% for gallstone pancreatitis.
Incorrect. Alcohol is the second most common cause, but a high ALT points to a biliary cause.
Incorrect. Nothing here suggests it; the ALT rise is the biliary clue.

options.text: Cannot be inferred, because ALT has no value for cause
options.rationale: Incorrect. A high ALT is specific for gallstones; it is a normal ALT that does not exclude them.

questions.stem: Which Ranson criterion is assessed within the first 48 hours rather than at admission?

options.rationale: Correct. Calcium is one of the six criteria measured within 48 hours.
Incorrect. LDH is an admission criterion.
Incorrect. WBC is an admission criterion.
Incorrect. Age is an admission criterion.

questions.stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis has a normal ALT and a lipase-to-amylase ratio of 4. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: Neither result settles the cause: a normal ALT does not exclude gallstones and the ratio only hints at alcohol
options.rationale: Correct. ALT is insensitive (about 48% in one study) and the ratio had a pooled specificity of only about 63%.

options.text: Gallstones are excluded because the ALT is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. ALT above 150 IU/L is specific but insensitive, so a normal value does not exclude gallstones.

options.text: Alcohol is confirmed because the ratio is above 3
options.rationale: Incorrect. The ratio has only moderate accuracy; it suggests, not confirms.

options.text: Order a urine amylase to identify the cause
options.rationale: Incorrect. Urine amylase has been studied for diagnosing pancreatitis, not for identifying its cause, and a 2025 meta-analysis found it no better than serum amylase.

references.citation: Shah AP, Mourad MM, Bramhall SR. Acute pancreatitis: current perspectives on diagnosis and management. J Inflamm Res. 2018;11:77-85. doi:10.2147/JIR.S135751
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). ALT > 150 IU/L predicts a biliary cause; a meta-analysis found this threefold elevation has a PPV of 95% for gallstone pancreatitis; about 50% of cases are gallstone-related.

references.citation: Hazem ZM. Acute biliary pancreatitis: diagnosis and treatment. Saudi J Gastroenterol. 2009;15(3):147-155. doi:10.4103/1319-3767.54740
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin reviewed to separate biliary from other causes; ALT > 150 IU/L specificity 96%, sensitivity 48%, so a normal ALT does not exclude gallstones; Ranson mortality rises with criteria count.

references.citation: Ekka NM, Kujur AD, Guria R, et al. Serum Lipase Amylase Ratio as an Indicator to Differentiate Alcoholic From Non-alcoholic Acute Pancreatitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Cureus. 2023;15(2):e35618. doi:10.7759/cureus.35618
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). Alcohol second most common cause after gallstones; L/A ratio proposed by Gumaste 1991; seven of nine included studies used a cut-off of 3 (two used 2); Results and abstract give pooled sensitivity 74% (95% CI 62-83%) and specificity 63% (95% CI 47-77%), moderate accuracy (the Discussion restates these as 75% and 56%, an internal inconsistency; the lesson uses the Results figures); post-test probability 50% to 67%.

references.citation: McCarrick CA, Singaravelu A, Al Rasheed A, Murphy R. Evaluating the Role of Urinary Amylase in Diagnosing Acute Pancreatitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Cureus. 2025;17(12):e98982. doi:10.7759/cureus.98982
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). Urine amylase follows serum amylase and remains elevated longer; pooled sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.86 at a model-derived 1,373 IU/L; does not appear to outperform serum amylase; utility in delayed or atypical presentations unsubstantiated.

references.citation: Abu-Eshy SA, Abolfotouh MA, Nawar E, Abu Sabib AR. Ranson’s criteria for acute pancreatitis in high altitude: do they need to be modified? Saudi J Gastroenterol. 2008;14(1):20-23. doi:10.4103/1319-3767.37797
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). Table 1: the 11 Ranson criteria (5 at admission, 6 during the initial 48 h) with cut-offs; fewer than 3 = mild, 3 or more = severe.

references.citation: Lee DW, Cho CM. Predicting Severity of Acute Pancreatitis. Medicina (Kaunas). 2022;58(6):787. doi:10.3390/medicina58060787
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). Table 4: non-biliary and biliary Ranson cut-offs (biliary: age > 70, WBC > 18,000, LDH > 400, glucose > 220, BUN rise > 2, fluid > 4 L); one point each; needs admission and 48-h data, limiting early prediction.

references.citation: Hu JX, Zhao CF, Wang SL, et al. Acute pancreatitis: A review of diagnosis, severity prediction and prognosis assessment from imaging technology, scoring system and artificial intelligence. World J Gastroenterol. 2023;29(37):5268-5291. doi:10.3748/wjg.v29.i37.5268
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). About 40% of serum amylase derives from the pancreas, the rest mainly from salivary glands.

references.citation: Skude G. Pancreatic Isoamylase as a Routine Test. EJIFCC. 2000;12(1):23-34.
references.usedFor: Full text read (Europe PMC). Salivary and pancreatic isoamylases contribute roughly equally to normal plasma amylase activity.

claims.text: Gallstones most common cause (about half), alcohol second; liver tests reviewed for biliary cause.
ALT > 150 IU/L (about 3×): PPV ~95% for gallstones; specificity 96%, sensitivity 48%; normal ALT does not exclude.
Lipase/amylase ratio (cut-off ~3): pooled sensitivity 74%, specificity 63% (Results; Discussion says 75%/56%); moderate accuracy.
Urine amylase follows serum and stays elevated longer; not better than serum amylase; late-presenter value unproven.
Serum amylase is salivary plus pancreatic (pancreatic about 40% to roughly half).
Ranson: 5 admission and 6 48-hour criteria with cut-offs; 1 point each; ≥ 3 severe; biliary version differs; needs 48 h.
Urine amylase > 1000 Somogyi units/hour almost exclusive to pancreatitis; AST alone > 3× ULN as a gallstone marker; lipase/amylase ratio cut-off > 5.
claims.note: Reviewer figures not found in the sources read; not taught as facts.

claims.text: “GA-LAW at the door, C-HOBBS by 48 hours.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 23 Hit 6 says AST/ALT > 3× ULN means gallstones are the cause in 95% of cases. Shah 2018 gives this for ALT > 150 IU/L (PPV 95%, meta-analysis), and Hazem 2009 reports sensitivity of only 48%, so a normal ALT does not exclude gallstones; the lesson teaches the ALT form with its insensitivity (register flag rv-ap-alt-gallstone-sensitivity).

Ch. 23 Hit 6 gives a lipase/amylase ratio > 5 with low sensitivity for alcohol. The Ekka 2023 meta-analysis assessed a cut-off of about 3 and found pooled sensitivity 74% and specificity 63% (its Discussion restates 75%/56%); the lesson teaches the meta-analysed cut-off and treats the ratio as a hint (register flag rv-ap-lipase-amylase-ratio-cutoff).

Ch. 23 Hit 7 lists one Ranson set. Lee 2022 shows these are the non-gallstone cut-offs and that a separate gallstone set uses different values (age > 70, WBC > 18,000, LDH > 400, glucose > 220, BUN rise > 2, fluid > 4 L) (register flag rv-ranson-biliary-version).

Ch. 23 Hit 4 says urine amylase is useful in late presenters, with > 1000 Somogyi units/hour almost exclusive to pancreatitis. The McCarrick 2025 meta-analysis found urine amylase no better than serum amylase and its utility in delayed presentations unsubstantiated; the Somogyi figure was not verified and is not taught (register flag rv-urine-amylase-late-presenters).
